title: Exploring the Association Between Breast Cancer Perception and Health-Promoting Lifestyle Behaviours Among Women: A Cross-Sectional Study in Saudi Arabia
abstract: Aim: To examine breast cancer perception, health-promoting lifestyle behaviours, and screening practices, and their sociodemographic and psychosocial correlates, among women in Abha, Saudi Arabia. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 1,002 women aged ≥18 years in Abha (May–December 2025), recruited online through social media and instant messaging. Validated Arabic versions of the Breast Cancer Perception Scale (BCPS) and HPLP-II were self-administered online, with self-reported breast self-examination (BSE), clinical breast examination (CBE), and mammography history. Multiple linear regression identified predictors of HPLP-II and BCPS scores. Results: Perceived knowledge (3.64 ± 1.05), treatment belief (3.43 ± 0.77), fear (3.25 ± 1.30), and perceived risk (3.40 ± 0.89) were moderately high; perceived need for health checks (2.78 ± 1.23) and stigma (2.89 ± 1.14) were lower. HPLP-II mean was 2.63 ± 0.46 (spiritual growth highest 2.96 ± 0.50; physical ac-tivity lowest 2.23 ± 0.60). Ever-screening: BSE 61.1% (95% CI 58.1–64.1), CBE 22.5% (95% CI 20.0–25.1), mammography 12.8% (95% CI 10.8–14.8). Perceived knowledge (β = 0.059), treatment belief (β = 0.120), and stigma (β = 0.058) were positively, and perceived need for health checks (β = −0.259), perceived risk (β = −0.130), and fear (β = −0.028) negatively, associated with HPLP-II. Married women had higher lifestyle and perception scores; more educated and publicly employed women had higher perception scores. Conclusion: Despite moderately high perceived knowledge, clinical screening particularly mammography remains very low, and physical activity, a modifiable breast cancer risk factor, is the weakest lifestyle do-main. Awareness alone does not translate into screening; interventions should address fear and symptom-contingent care-seeking, embed screening referral in primary care, involve families, and promote culturally appropriate physical activity.

Ever-screening: BSE 61.1% (95% CI 58.1–64.1), CBE 22.5% (95% CI 20.0–25.1), mammography 12.8% (95% CI 10.8–14.8). Married women had higher lifestyle and perception scores; more educated and publicly employed women had higher perception scores.

Conclusion:

Despite moderately high perceived knowledge, clinical screening particularly mammography remains very low, and physical activity, a modifiable breast cancer risk factor, is the weakest lifestyle do-main. Awareness alone does not translate into screening; interventions should address fear and symptom-contingent care-seeking, embed screening referral in primary care, involve families, and promote culturally appropriate physical activity.

title: A Controlled Benchmark of Deep Segmentation Architectures for Mammographic Microcalcification Segmentation on CBIS-DDSM: Evidence Consistent with an Annotation-Related Performance Limit
abstract: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women worldwide, and clustered microcalcifications on mammography are among its earliest indicators. Automated segmentation of microcalcifications is challenging because the calcifications are small, sparse, and often embedded in dense fibroglandular tissue. In addition, publicly available datasets such as CBIS-DDSM provide annotations at the calcification-cluster level rather than for individual calcification particles. Although numerous deep-learning architectures have been proposed for this task, their relative performance under a common experimental framework remains unclear. This study presents a rigorous, leakage-controlled benchmark of ten segmentation architectures, including convolutional models (U-Net, nnU-Net, BreastNet, ConvNeXt-UNet), an attention-gated model (Attention U-Net), convolution-transformer hybrids (TransUNet, Swin-UNet, MedFormer, UNETR), and MAFT-Net, a multi-scale attention network incorporating dilated convolutions, squeeze-and-excitation gating, self-attention, and gated feature fusion. All models were trained from scratch using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimisation, and patient-disjoint train/test partitions on the CBIS-DDSM calcification subset. Performance was evaluated using Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), Intersection-over-Union (IoU), 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and classification AUC. Across all architectures, Dice scores were confined to a narrow range (0.076-0.114), with most pairwise differences failing to reach statistical significance. Increasing architectural complexity, including transformer-based models containing up to 89 million parameters, did not produce consistent performance gains. ROI occupancy analysis showed a strong positive association between Dice and annotation size, with mean Dice increasing from 0.023 to 0.255 across occupancy quartiles. These findings suggest that segmentation performance on CBIS-DDSM is influenced more by the region-level annotation format than by architectural innovation, highlighting an important limitation when interpreting reported overlap metrics.

title: Case Series Analysis of Five Rare Cases of Hyperprolactinemia in Diabetes Mellitus: Clinical Characteristics, Molecular Pathways, and Implications for Targeted Management
abstract: Background: Hyperprolactinemia, characterized by serum prolactin levels >20 ng/mL, is a rare comorbidity in diabetes mellitus, potentially exacerbating insulin resistance and glycemic dysregulation via JAK/STAT signaling. This case series analysis examines five rare cases to elucidate clinical patterns, molecular mechanisms, and therapeutic outcomes, aiming to inform precision endocrine management. Methods: Five cases were curated from PubMed and Scopus (1999–2025), focusing on hyperprolactinemia in diabetes (type 1, type 2, or insipidus). Data on demographics, symptoms, laboratory findings (prolactin, insulin, C-peptide), imaging (MRI), and treatment outcomes were extracted. Results: The cohort included 3 females and 2 males (mean age: 26.2 years, range: 7–33). Prolactin levels ranged from 145–3,177 ng/mL, with 2/5 cases (40%) having type 1 diabetes, 1/5 (20%) type 2, 1/5 (20%) diabetes insipidus, and 1/5 (20%) factitious hypoglycemia. Presentations included hypogonadism (3/5, 60%), galactorrhea (2/5, 40%), and hypoglycemia (2/5, 40%). MRI revealed microadenomas (2/5, 40%), a macroadenoma (1/5, 20%), or normal pituitary (2/5, 40%). Cabergoline or medication withdrawal normalized prolactin in 4/5 (80%), reducing levels (e.g., 3,177 to 321 ng/mL in one case) and improving glycemic control (fewer hypoglycemic episodes) in 3/5 (60%). Prolactin activates JAK2/STAT5, inducing SOCS3 to inhibit IRS-1/PI3K/Akt, impairing glucose uptake. Conclusion: Hyperprolactinemia, whether tumoral or non-tumoral, disrupts metabolic homeostasis in diabetes. Routine prolactin screening is recommended for patients with reproductive or glycemic anomalies, emphasizing targeted therapies like dopamine agonists to optimize outcomes.

title: Clinical Applications of Metabolomics in Paediatric Brain Tumours and Other Solid Tumours: A Review
abstract: There is growing interest in utilising metabolomics as a tool in childhood cancer research. We propose four main applications of metabolomics in this context; as a less invasive diagnostic technique, to identify prognostic biomarkers, to monitor disease progression or detect relapse and to identify novel therapeutic targets. MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane databases were searched. Studies evaluating metabolomics in paediatric brain and other solid tumours in the context of our four applications were included. Studies evaluating other ‘omics’ modalities, tumour types, outcomes or involving adults were excluded. 39 articles were included. Published evidence in brain tumours includes the potential for metabolomics to identify biomarkers from peripheral blood samples, possibly obviating the need for invasive biopsies. Additionally, magnetic resonance spectroscopy adds value to conventional magnetic resonance imaging for diagnosis and prognostication. Considering other solid tumours, metabolomics has been evaluated in neuroblastoma for risk stratification of disease and in osteosarcoma, retinoblastoma, Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma for identifying novel diagnostic biomarkers and improving understanding of tumour pathophysiology. Our review highlights the wide-ranging applications of metabolomics across paediatric brain and other solid tumours. There is an emerging role for metabolomics within research and clinical spheres to improve the diagnosis and management of childhood cancers.

title: OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound): A Multiorgan Bedside Ultrasound Framework for Obesity Phenotyping
abstract: Obesity is a heterogeneous chronic disease in which cardiometabolic and functional risks are influenced not only by total body fat but also by its anatomical distribution, ectopic fat accumulation, and skeletal muscle quality. Traditional anthropometric measurements, such as body mass index and waist circumference, fail to capture these biological differences. Point-of-care ultrasound provides a portable, radiation-free, repeatable, and widely available bedside tool for assessing multiple adipose and muscular compartments, yet a broadly standardized framework integrating these measurements into a multiorgan obesity phenotype remains lacking. We propose OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound), a pragmatic multiorgan point-of-care ultrasound framework for structured obesity phenotyping. To facilitate competency-based and stepwise implementation, OBESUS comprises two complementary tiers: OBESUS-Core evaluates abdominal subcutaneous adiposity, preperitoneal fat thickness, hepatic steatosis, and rectus femoris muscle quality, whereas OBESUS-Plus incorporates epicardial and perirenal adipose tissue as additional cardiorenal ectopic fat depots. Rather than generating a numerical score, the framework integrates these findings into four non-mutually exclusive ultrasound-derived phenotypes: metabolic, myosteatotic, epicardial adiposity, and perirenal adiposity. This narrative review describes the conceptual basis, standardized acquisition methodology, pragmatic reference thresholds, and potential clinical applications of OBESUS. The framework is intended to provide a foundation for prospective evaluation of its reproducibility, clinical validity, prognostic significance and potential utility for longitudinal monitoring.

title: Molecular PET Imaging Versus Conventional Imaging for Detection of Mandibular Metastases in Prostate Cancer: A Paired Retrospective Study
abstract: Purpose: Maxillofacial metastases from prostate cancer are accounts for 9–11% of metastatic jaw lesions. Optimal imaging for suspected maxillofacial metastases remains undefined. Conventional imaging often lacks sensitivity for early disease, while PET/CT may be limited due to physiologic tracer uptake in adjacent salivary glands. With increasing use of PET/CT in advanced prostate cancer, its diagnostic performance in the mandibular region requires further evaluation. Methods: We conducted a single-institution paired retrospective study using the prospectively maintained Mayo Clinic Advanced Prostate Cancer Registry. Patients with clinically confirmed mandibular metastases who underwent molecular PET/CT ([⁶⁸Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 or [¹¹C]choline) and conventional imaging (CT or MRI) within 1 month were included. All studies were blindly reviewed by a board-certified radiologist specialized in nuclear medicine. Detection rates, anatomic distribution, and quantitative imaging parameters were assessed. paired detection rates were compared using a one-sided exact McNemar test, with a two-sided exact test performed as a sensitivity analysis. Results: Eighteen patients with clinically confirmed mandibular metastases underwent 36 paired imaging evaluations (18 molecular PET/CT and 18 conventional studies). Median age was 70.5 years (IQR, 60–77), and median Gleason score was 8 (IQR, 7–9). At detection of mandibular metastasis, 56% of our cohort had hormone-sensitive and 44% had castration-resistant disease. Molecular PET/CT detected mandibular involvement in 18/18 patients (100%; 95% CI, 81–100%) versus 13/18 (72.2%; 95% CI, 47–90%) with conventional imaging. All five discordant cases were detected by molecular PET/CT but not conventional imaging, with no discordant cases favoring conventional imaging (one-sided exact McNemar p = 0.031; two-sided p = 0.063). Mandibular involvement was predominantly unilateral (94.4%), most commonly involving the body (50%), followed by the ramus (28%) and condyle (17%). Median SUVmax was 6.3 (IQR, 4.4–16.9) for PSMA PET/CT and 4.3 (IQR, 3.8–8.5) for choline PET/CT; median lesion volume was 5.0 mL (IQR, 1.1–11.3). Conclusions: Molecular PET/CT identified all clinically confirmed mandibular prostate cancer metastases in this paired cohort, including five cases not detected by conventional imaging. Despite physiologic tracer uptake in adjacent salivary structures, mandibular metastatic disease remained detectable on molecular imaging. These findings suggest that molecular PET/CT may provide complementary value when mandibular metastasis is suspected, particularly when conventional imaging is negative or equivocal.

title: Expander-Assisted Immediate Implant Placement in a Maxillary Lateral Incisor Site Combining Apical Bone Expansion, Supramaxillary Arch Buttress Stabilization, and Immediate Provisionalization: A Case Report
abstract: Background: Replacement of a maxillary lateral incisor is among the most demanding indications in implant dentistry. The site is typically narrow bucco-palatally, the buccal plate is frequently thin and largely bundle-bone dependent, and the aesthetic tolerance for ridge collapse is minimal. Immediate (Type 1) placement shortens treatment and preserves the soft-tissue architecture, but it does not prevent the remodelling of the buccal wall that follows extraction, and the osteotomy itself risks fenestration or loss of primary stability. Case presentation. A 60-year-old male smoker (about 20 cigarettes/day) with a history of stage IV periodontitis presented with an unrestorable, almost circumferential carious lesion of the maxillary left lateral incisor, already restored with a metal-ceramic crown (FDI 22). After atraumatic flapless extraction, the osteotomy was initiated on the palatal wall of the socket with a lance bur and a 2.2 mm pilot drill, and completed with a sequence of screw bone expanders instead of rotary drills. Expander position and axis were verified intraoperatively with a periapical radiograph and a CBCT scan before the osteotomy was finalized. An implant (“Newton”, Kalodon, 4.25 × 13 mm) was placed in a palatally shifted position with apical bone expansion of the nasal-floor cortex (part of the “supramaxillary arch buttress”, a nomenclature we have proposed), achieving an insertion torque exceeding 60 Ncm. The residual buccal gap was filled with a deproteinized bovine bone mineral xenograft to compensate for the expected resorption of the bundle bone, and a screw-retained provisional restoration was delivered the same day. Healing was uneventful. At three months the peri-implant mucosa was stable and well contoured, with no visible collapse of the buccal contour; the site was digitally scanned and a definitive screw-retained zirconia crown was delivered. Radiographically, the marginal bone level appeared stable at all controls. The patient was then followed for 12 months after crown delivery, with an uneventful course. Conclusions. In a narrow lateral incisor socket, combining “apical expansion” with immediate implant placement, buccal gap grafting and immediate provisionalization allowed a single-surgery, three-month rehabilitation with preserved mucosal architecture. Intraoperative three-dimensional verification of the expander before finalizing the osteotomy was decisive in confirming the implant axis in a site with minimal (bundle) buccal bone. The result was obtained in a heavy smoker with a history of severe periodontitis and should be confirmed with quantitative, longer-term data. Engaging the “supramaxillary arch buttress” of the splanchnocranium ensures the necessary stability.

title: Esophageal Injury During Transesophageal Echocardiography-Guided Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Narrative Review
abstract: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains an established imaging modality for guiding percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), providing real-time visualization during transseptal puncture, device deployment and procedural assessment. However, esophageal instrumentation and prolonged probe manipulation may result in gastrointestinal injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing esophageal abnormalities or increased bleeding risk. This narrative review summarizes the available evidence regarding the mechanisms, risk factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, management and prevention of TEE-associated esophageal injury during LAAO while examining alternative imaging strategies. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by targeted searches of broader structural heart intervention literature. Although clinically recognized TEE-associated gastrointestinal complications are uncommon, studies employing systematic endoscopic surveillance have identified substantially higher rates of subclinical mucosal injury. Reported manifestations range from transient dysphagia and superficial mucosal lesions to gastrointestinal bleeding, intramural esophageal hematoma, perforation and fistula formation. Nevertheless, limited LAAO-specific evidence, heterogeneous outcome definitions and differences in surveillance strategies preclude reliable estimation of procedure-specific esophageal injury incidence. Intracardiac echocardiography eliminates esophageal instrumentation but carries a distinct procedural risk profile, whereas cardiac computed tomography (CCT) provides complementary opportunities for preprocedural planning and postprocedural surveillance. Careful preprocedural assessment, judicious probe manipulation, early recognition of complications and individualized imaging selection are important considerations. Prospective studies incorporating standardized esophageal injury endpoints are needed to establish the true clinical burden and guide preventive strategies.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Medical Image Analysis in Low-Resource Settings
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for medical image analysis is increasingly being developed for low-resource settings, where specialist expertise, imaging equipment, labelled data, and computing resources may be limited. We systematically reviewed 189 studies published between January 2021 and January 2026 to examine how these constraints relate to imaging modalities, clinical applications, and AI methods in low-resource settings. Each study was also assessed against 15 criteria adapted from the FUTURE-AI principles for trustworthy AI. Shortages of clinical expertise were the most common constraint, and portable or lower-cost imaging was widely used. Transfer learning was the most frequent technical strategy (59%), followed by data augmentation (54%) and efficient model design (36%). Medical-image pretraining and self-supervised learning were each used in 4% of studies, and model compression in 3%. Applications were concentrated in retinal disease, pulmonary disease, antenatal care, parasitic diseases, and cervical screening. Beyond these technical and clinical patterns, the trustworthy AI assessment showed a clear gap between documenting how systems were developed and demonstrating how they performed under relevant local conditions. Subgroup performance was evaluated in 24% of studies, intended users or realistic working conditions in 25%, and model explanations with intended users in 4%. Consistent with this gap, among 15 studies that reported the same model and metric during development and in the local setting, 12 performed worse locally. Future research should prioritise representative local evaluation, intended-user assessment, demonstrated resource suitability, and reproducible research practices.

title: Most Colon Grading Mistakes Are Neighbors: Adjacent-Grade Error Shares and Grade-3 Recall on Public Histopathology Embeddings
abstract: Colon histology computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) papers often lead with pooled grading accuracy. That number mixes easy majority-class hits with minority-class misses and treats a Grade 1↔Grade 2 swap as interchangeable with calling poorly differentiated cancer well differentiated. This preprint recomputes stratified five-fold support-vector grading on 560 public colorectal cancer patches with frozen ResNet50 embeddings (Grade 1 n=251, Grade 2 n=210, Grade 3 n=99). Cross-validated accuracy is 73.6% ± 2.9% and macro-F1 is 0.705, but Grade 3 recall is only 0.475. Of 148 residual mistakes, 119 (80.4%) are adjacent-grade swaps; 29 (19.6%) jump from Grade 3 to Grade 1. title: Synergistic Therapeutic Effects of Non-Invasive Aesthetic Technologies and Applied Sports Activity in the Management of Localized Adiposity and Cellulite
abstract: Non-invasive aesthetic technologies, such as cryolipolysis (CLL), radiofrequency (RF), and ultrasound cavitation, have become standard therapeutic approaches for the management of localized adiposity and gynoid lipodystrophy (cellulite). While these technologies effectively induce adipocyte apoptosis or lipolysis, the subsequent clearance of cellular debris and free fatty acids (FFAs) heavily relies on the body’s lymphatic and metabolic pathways. This article explores the therapeutic synergy between applied physical activity and non-invasive body contouring. We hypothesize that integrating targeted exercise—specifically aerobic training and targeted muscle contractions—may act as a therapeutic adjunct to aesthetic sections. Physiologically, exercise-induced muscle pumps accelerate lymphatic drainage, facilitating the rapid removal of metabolic byproducts, while increased energy expenditure promotes the oxidation of released FFAs, preventing their re-esterification. By bridging aesthetic science and applied physical activity, this paper proposes a theoretical framework for combined protocols, intended to guide future clinical investigation and offer a holistic, therapeutic approach to body sculpting.

title: A Rare Presentation of Acute-Onset BCG-Induced Aortic Aneurysm: A Case Report
abstract: Background: Mycotic Aortic aneurysms (MAA) are saccular aneurysms of the infected aortic wall. Mycobacterium, compared with other bacteria, is less likely to cause MAA; most cases follow, but it is a rare, late, systemic, and serious complication of intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) instillation for bladder cancer. Case Presentation: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, diabetic foot ulcer with methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) bacteremia, status post partial toe amputation, and papillary urothelial carcinoma treated with transurethral resection and intravesical BCG instillation, recently underwent a computed tomography (CT) abdomen 2 weeks ago for abdominal pain, which revealed colonic stool without other pathological findings, who currently presented with worsening abdominal pain, and the CT scan identified a new 2.5-centimeter pseudoaneurysm of the infrarenal aorta, associated with a periaortic and aortocaval mass, likely a hematoma, infectious mycotic aneurysm, or neoplastic process. The patient received intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for presumed MSSA, a potential cause of a mycotic aneurysm, which was later discontinued after negative blood cultures. Vascular surgery consultation led to endovascular aortic stenting. Infectious disease recommended a Karius test; despite no warning signs, it returned positive for the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and a diagnosis of a BCG-induced aneurysm was made. The patient was treated with isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyridoxine, then continued isoniazid and rifampin for 9 months. Conclusion: We presented a rare case of a BCG-induced mycotic aortic aneurysm that developed within 2 weeks. Therefore, we need a low threshold for MAA in patients with a history of intravesical BCG instillations who present with worsening abdominal pain, even if prior imaging 2 weeks ago showed no warning signs and instillations were given 2 years ago. Testing and diagnosing a BCG-induced aneurysm are necessary despite endovascular intervention, because it can further infect the stent and form an abscess if untreated.

title: Pulmonary Alveolar Microlithiasis: From Clinicopathologic Description to Molecular Pathogenesis and Emerging Therapies
abstract: Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis (PAM) is a rare autosomal recessive lung disease in which calcium phosphate microliths fill the alveoli. Although the cause of it remained unknown for some time, more recently loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2, which encodes the sodium-phosphate cotransporter NPT2b, explain nearly all genetically tested cases; failure to clear phosphate from the alveolar lining fluid leads to microlith formation, and an epithelial Npt2b-knockout mouse reproduces the human phenotype. Diagnosis now rests mainly on characteristic high-resolution CT and, increasingly, on genotyping rather than lung biopsy. The protracted course has been described in some series of cases, with death from respiratory failure. No drug has proven efficacy; lung transplantation is the only established therapy, and no allograft recurrence has been documented. Preclinical data support phosphate restriction, EDTA lavage and gene-directed approaches. However, controlled trials with more genotype-phenotype correlation and prospective natural-history data are still needed.

title: Gastric Fungal Colonization as a Candidate Mechanism in ALS-Spectrum Motor Neuron Disease: A Hypothesis Supported by Five Years of Case Documentation
abstract: Background: The etiology of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) remains unknown in approximately 90% of cases [1]. A unified mechanism linking environmental mycotoxin exposure, gut-brain axis dysfunction, and motor neuron disease has not been systematically investigated. Hypothesis. Chronic colonization of the gastric mucosa by a mycotoxin-producing mold, concealed beneath a mucosal biofilm and therefore potentially undetectable by standard endoscopy, is proposed to drive sustained motor-neuron hyperexcitability through three concurrent mechanisms: (1) TLR activation on vagal afferent fibers projecting excitatory signals to brainstem motor nuclei via neural spill-over; (2) cross-reactive immune attack on motor-neuron surface proteins via molecular mimicry; and (3) Dectin-1-mediated neuroinflammation during biofilm disruption. Case. Five-year index case: five positive urinary Trichothecene assays including one after a 32-hour fast (internal source confirmed); six immunological assessments, including five CD25 measurements, showing markedly reduced measured T-cell activation markers and cytokine responses (CD25 1.0–3.1%, reference 13–24%; IFN-γ 79.5 pg/ml, reference ≥118; IL-17 5.4 pg/ml, reference ≥9.6); EMG-confirmed neurogenic remodeling followed by documented stabilization; over 30 reproducible pharmacological observations consistent with the proposed mechanism; and formal diagnostic exclusion across four institutions over three years. Implications. Convergent findings from the published literature, together with more than 30 internally consistent pharmacological observations, support formal investigation of the proposed model. Proposed initial investigations include urinary mycotoxin testing, lymphocyte transformation testing, mycotoxin antibody testing, visual contrast sensitivity screening, and biofilm-directed endoscopy with confocal laser endomicroscopy, targeted biopsy, and PCR analysis.

title: Biologically Inspired Selective Attention for Prostate MRI: A Segmentation-Guided Vision Transformer Framework for Computer-Aided Diagnosis
abstract: Prostate cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed malignancy in men, yet interpretation of multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) suffers from substantial inter-observer variability and depends on scarce expert radiologists. Expert readers follow a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine visual strategy: they first localize the prostate gland and then direct focused attention to tissue within it. Inspired by this biological selective-attention mechanism, we propose a segmentation-guided framework in which a modality-aware 3D Vision Transformer (ViT) first delineates the prostate gland from T2-weighted, ADC, and DWI volumes, and the resulting anatomical mask then constrains downstream cancer detection. Global self-attention models long-range anatomical context, analogous to the integration of peripheral and foveal information in human vision. Detection was evaluated through two pathways: gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) texture features with classical classifiers, and a ViT classifier. On 200 patients from the public PROSTATEx cohort, the proposed segmentation model achieved a Dice similarity coefficient of [0.905] versus [0.831] for an optimized U-Net. The segmentation-guided ViT achieved an AUC of [0.987] and an accuracy of [0.998] for clinically significant cancer detection. Ablation experiments confirmed that anatomical guidance improved both pathways. These results show that emulating expert visual search strategies yields accurate and interpretable computer-aided prostate cancer diagnosis.

title: DeepSUM-DWI: A Joint Image Registration and Super-Resolution Convolutional Neural Network for Diffusion-Weighted MRI
abstract: Background: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is an important MRI technique for studying tissue microstructure and structural connectivity, but is limited by relatively low spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and sensitivity to inter-acquisition motion. A deep-learning framework was developed that jointly performs image registration and super-resolution on repeated low-resolution DWI inputs to generate a single registered, higher apparent spatial-resolution output. Methods: DeepSUM-DWI adapts a DeepSUM multi-image super-resolution architecture for repeated DWI. It comprises a shared 2D super-resolution feature extractor (SISRNet), a registration network (RegNet), and a 3D fusion network (FusionNet). Evaluation used (1) simulated repetitions with synthetic motion, (2) retrospectively downsampled acquisitions from 12 subjects, and (3) a prospective dual-resolution example with matched 1.0 × 1.0 and 2.0 × 2.0 mm² acquisitions. Results: DeepSUM-DWI reconstructed a single high-resolution-appearing DWI image from multiple low-resolution repetitions while preserving structural characteristics of the high-resolution acquisitions. The model remained robust across synthetic motion magnitudes. In retrospectively downsampled data, it improved NRMSE by 71–79% and PSNR by 10.6–13.5 dB, for super-resolution factors of 2–3, relative to averaging interpolated low-resolution images, with a mean SSIM > 0.99. In prospectively acquired data, it recovered finer structures than visible in the acquired low-resolution images while maintaining contrast consistency. Exploratory diffusion analysis suggested that some gains in apparent detail propagated to FA maps. Conclusions: DeepSUM-DWI provides a framework for joint registration and super-resolution of repeated DWI acquisitions, with potential to improve apparent spatial resolution while retaining the SNR benefits of repeated acquisition.

title: Biomechanical Evaluation of Uterine Morphology and Tissue Mechanical Properties in a Computational Model of the Pelvic Cavity
abstract: Female pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a gynecological disorder characterized by pelvic organ descent that significantly impacts quality of life. With increasing global burden, approaches for early diagnosis are essential. This study illustrates a patient-specific computational model of the pelvic cavity, updating the uterine and cervical geometric model and assigning cervical tissue properties. Three distinct uterine geometric models were assembled, based on literature measurements and magnetic resonance images for comparison and validation. Human cervical properties were extrapolated from biomechanical testing of ovine pelvic tissues. Finite elements simulations of the Valsalva maneuver were conducted to analyze the biomechanical effects of varying uterine morphology and tissue properties on the pelvic cavity, including the bladder neck, vagina, and uterosacral ligaments (USLs). Results show that a uterus with softer properties assigned exhibits less vertical displacement and relies more on USLs support than a stiffer one. Furthermore, uterine volume and morphology significantly influence pelvic dynamics: a larger uterus tends toward anteversion, while a smaller uterus increases vertical vaginal displacement (10.57 mm vs 6.04 mm) and requires greater USLs support. Anatomical variations directly constrain bladder neck displacement. These computational advancements aim to enhance patient-specific modeling, assisting clinical decision-making.

title: From Manual to Machine: Development and Internal Validation of an NLP-Based Prediction Model for Brain Death Using Admission CT Reports, 2011–2024
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Early identification of patients progressing toward brain death may reduce missed organ donation opportunities. We aimed to develop and internally validate an interpretable natural language processing (NLP) model using admission brain computed tomog-raphy (CT) reports. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included 163 adults ad-mitted between 2011 and 2024 with acute neurological injury; 96 subsequently fulfilled brain death criteria and 67 did not. Predictors were derived exclusively from admission CT report text using rule-based preprocessing and term frequency–inverse document frequency word 1–3-gram features. Logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and support vector machine models were evaluated using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation with 20 repetitions. Vectorization, cal-ibration, model fitting, and threshold selection were restricted to training folds. A prespecified sensitivity target of at least 95% guided threshold selection. Interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). RESULTS: XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.807 (95% confidence in-terval, 0.793–0.820) and a pooled out-of-fold value of 0.791. At the high-sensitivity operating point, mean sensitivity was 0.947 and specificity was 0.275. SHAP identified clinically plausible descriptors related to cerebral edema, mass effect, ventricular distortion, ischemic injury, and midline abnormalities. CONCLUSIONS: Admission CT reports contain prognostic information that can be extracted using NLP to support earlier identification of patients at risk of progression to brain death and potential organ donation. External multicenter validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Study on the Value of pH-Responsive Probes in Evaluating Acidic Environment Changes During Chronic Liver Disease Progression in Rats
abstract: During the progression of chronic liver disease, changes in the acidic microenvironment of liver tissue are closely correlated with the extent of pathological injury, making precise monitoring of these changes critical for disease assessment. Traditional detection methods (e.g., blood gas analysis, tissue pH electrodes) suffer from limitations such as high invasiveness and low spatiotemporal resolution, hindering dynamic reflection of hepatic acid environment evolution. PH-responsive probes (e.g., fluorescent probes, magnetic resonance probes), leveraging their non-invasive, real-time, and high-specificity advantages, have emerged as a research focus in this field. This review focuses on the application of such probes in rat chronic liver disease models: outlining their design principles and types, analyzing their quantitative detection capabilities for liver acidification levels, summarizing their value in correlating pathological processes such as liver inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, and demonstrating their ability to identify disease progression and evaluate intervention efficacy through early detection of acidic environment changes. Studies indicate that pH-responsive probes provide a tool for elucidating the mechanisms of the acidic microenvironment in chronic liver disease and lay the foundation for developing non-invasive monitoring technologies in clinical translation, holding significant academic and practical value.

title: Brain Tumour Detection Using EfficientNet-Transformer Hybrid Network with SHAP and Grad-CAM Based Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Accurate and interpretable brain tumour detection from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains a significant challenge in computer-aided diagnosis. This study proposes an EfficientNet–Transformer Hybrid Network integrated with SHapley Additive ExPlanations (SHAP) and Grad-CAM explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques for automated and trustworthy brain tumour classification. Methods: The proposed framework combines EfficientNet for local feature extraction and a Vision Transformer for global contextual learning. MRI images from publicly available benchmark datasets containing four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, and no tumour) were preprocessed and augmented before training. The model was trained using an 80:20 training-testing split, while SHAP and Grad-CAM were employed to provide feature-level and spatial explanations of predictions. Results: The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of 98.88%, outperforming several state-of-the-art CNN and transformer models. It also attained average precision, recall, and F1-score values of 98.90%, 98.88%, and 98.89%, respectively, with an average AUC of 0.9893. Ablation and robustness analyses demonstrated that integrating SHAP and Grad-CAM improved interpretability while maintaining high predictive performance under noisy conditions. Conclusions: The proposed EfficientNet–Transformer framework effectively combines local and global feature learning with dual explainability mechanisms to deliver accurate and clinically interpretable brain tumour classification. The results demonstrate its potential as a reliable computer-aided diagnosis tool for neuro-oncology and clinical decision support systems.

title: Beyond the Classical Paradigm of Diabetic Kidney Disease (DKD): Evolving Phenotypes and the Role of Kidney Biopsy
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous condition encompassing distinct clinical and pathological phenotypes. Albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate may follow divergent trajectories, with non-albuminuric kidney function decline representing a common and clinically relevant phenotype. Importantly, clinical features do not always reflect the underlying renal pathology, as patients with diabetes may present with diabetic kidney disease, non-diabetic kidney disease (NDKD), or mixed lesions. Conventional clinical markers, including diabetic retinopathy, hematuria, proteinuria, and eGFR decline, modify but do not reliably establish the underlying diagnosis. Kidney biopsy therefore retains a selective but important role in patients with atypical or rapidly evolving presentations, particularly when histological findings may alter treatment or prognosis. Beyond diagnostic classification, biopsy can provide prognostic information through assessment of glomerular, tubulointerstitial, and vascular injury. Future approaches should integrate longitudinal clinical trajectories with histopathology and molecular profiling, positioning kidney biopsy as a bridge toward mechanism-based classification and precision medicine in DKD.

Importantly, clinical features do not always reflect the underlying renal pathology, as patients with diabetes may present with diabetic kidney disease, non-diabetic kidney disease (NDKD), or mixed lesions. Conventional clinical markers, including diabetic retinopathy, hematuria, proteinuria, and eGFR decline, modify but do not reliably establish the underlying diagnosis. Kidney biopsy therefore retains a selective but important role in patients with atypical or rapidly evolving presentations, particularly when histological findings may alter treatment or prognosis. Beyond diagnostic classification, biopsy can provide prognostic information through assessment of glomerular, tubulointerstitial, and vascular injury. Future approaches should integrate longitudinal clinical trajectories with histopathology and molecular profiling, positioning kidney biopsy as a bridge toward mechanism-based classification and precision medicine in DKD.

title: Binary Classification of Breast Cancer Images Using CNNs Enhanced by ALO-CLAHE-MSER Preprocessing
abstract: This work presents an intelligent image-processing framework for automatically detecting and clas-sifying benign and malignant regions in breast tissue by integrating Contrast Limited Adaptive His-togram Equalization (CLAHE), Maximally Stable Extremal Regions (MSER), and metaheuristic opti-mization algorithms. Identifying tumor-related regions in breast images is challenging because their visual characteristics can vary considerably with tissue density, illumination conditions, surface tex-ture, intensity distribution, lesion severity, and image acquisition conditions. These variations can make conventional image segmentation and manually configured MSER approaches sensitive to pa-rameter selection and less robust when detecting heterogeneous cancerous regions. To address these limitations, this study highlights the critical role of metaheuristic optimization as a key driver for fully automating and optimizing the combined CLAHE-MSER pipeline for binary breast cancer classifica-tion. Methods: First, CLAHE is applied to the input medical images to improve local contrast and enhance visual differences between healthy and cancerous tissue. The enhanced images are subse-quently processed using the MSER technique to identify stable intensity regions potentially associated with lesions or tumor masses. Rather than relying on manual configuration, the MSER parameter space and enhancement thresholds are formulated as a multidimensional optimization problem, and metaheuristic optimization algorithms are employed to automatically explore the parameter space and determine optimal configurations for region detection. Candidate solutions are iteratively evalu-ated using an objective function designed to improve the quality, stability, spatial coherence, and ac-curacy of the detected tumor regions prior to binary classification. The proposed metaheuristic-driven CLAHE-MSER framework therefore lets the detection process adapt automatically to the visual char-acteristics of individual medical images while eliminating dependence on manually selected parame-ters. Results: We performed experimental evaluations on medical images containing healthy, benign, and malignant regions. We quantitatively evaluated the performance of the proposed CLAHE-MSER framework, optimized by metaheuristic algorithms, using several image-quality, region-detection, and binary classification metrics. The experimental results indicate that incorporating CLAHE improves local contrast and facilitates the identification of subtle differences between healthy and affected tis-sue. Furthermore, metaheuristic optimization significantly improves MSER parameter selection, re-sulting in more consistent and spatially coherent detection of tumor regions than conventional MSER configurations and non-optimized approaches. The optimized configurations better preserve relevant cancer-related structures, maximizing overall binary classification accuracy while drastically reduc-ing the detection of healthy tissue and irrelevant regions. Conclusion: Integrating CLAHE- MSER, and metaheuristic optimization provides a robust, fully automated, and adaptive framework for binary breast cancer classification based on medical image analysis. CLAHE enhances the visual infor-mation needed to distinguish affected tissue, while MSER extracts stable image regions associated with potential tumor lesions. Metaheuristic optimization serves as the central component to automate and refine the detection process by dynamically identifying suitable parameter configurations for different image conditions. The proposed methodology represents a promising computational ap-proach for automated breast cancer screening, computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), lesion classification, and intelligent medical decision support systems.

title: Predictive Value of the Cincinnati Scale for Code Stroke Activation in Relation to CT Scan Findings
abstract: Background: Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide and main cause of disability in adults. Timely care is essential to achieve reperfusion and preserve brain tissue. Efforts have been made to correlate CT signs with the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale to activate the Comprehensive Stroke Protocol. Analyzing these factors may provide useful parameters for selection. Material and Methods: This analytical, cross-sectional, observational, prospective study was conducted at the Regional General Hospital in Orizaba, Mexico. A total of 497_20 non-contrast cranial CT scans were analyzed using PACS. Patients were followed through medical records until discharge diagnosis was confirmed. Data collection occurred from March 2024_45. Results: 497_2 CT scans were reviewed. The Stroke Code was most often used in the 70-79-year age group, with 56.9% female patients. Of 72_24 ischemic stroke cases, only 24_29 were within the therapeutic window. Conclusion: The Cincinnati scale as a rapid cerebrovascular screen has only moderate to low discriminatory ability. Sensitivity and positive predictive value are very low. Therefore, it is not suitable alone. The results provide opportunity to train doctors to use the Cincinnati scale alongside the NIHSS scale, which has better predictive ability. More public education is recommended to help patients present within the window.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Investigating Pseudo-Learning and Bias Propagation in MRI Brain Tumour Classification
abstract: A brain tumour is an abnormal growth of cells in the brain, which can be either benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous). The 5-year survival rate for benign brain tumours is approximately 85-95%, whereas it is only 35-36% for malignant tumours. Therefore, early detection and diagnosis of brain tumours is important. The recent developments in deep learning have allowed for high precision, accuracy, and automation in detecting these tumours, including both gliomas and pituitary tumours. In this paper, three deep learning-based models for brain tumour categorisation from MRI images are compared to understand the limitations of accuracy-based evaluation with metrics such as class-wise performance and Grad-CAM. To assess the performance and observe various behavioural issues of the models used in this analysis, the MRI scans from the Brain Tumour MRI Dataset from Kaggle and the BRISC 2025 classification dataset containing MRI images from all four major tumour groups were leveraged for their training and testing. The first model serves as a baseline EfficientNet classifier, while the second model applies fine-tuning techniques to improve feature learning. The third model further enhances performance by incorporating multi-dataset training to increase data diversity. The reported confusion matrices show that Model V3 achieved 97.63% accuracy on its 800-image test set. Because its test set differs in size and may differ in composition from those of Models V1 and V2, this result should not be interpreted as a direct like-for-like comparison.The findings highlight the importance of combining conventional performance metrics with Grad-CAM analysis when investigating model behaviour, while further evaluation is needed to establish whether multi-dataset training reduces pseudo-learning or improves generalisation.

title: Beyond 99%: Auditing Leakage, Shortcuts and Calibration in COVID-19 CT Classification
abstract: Public CT benchmarks for COVID-19 report slice-level accuracy above 99%, yet slices from one scan are near-duplicates and most datasets ship without patient IDs. We audit a MobileNetV3-Large classifier on a 19,685-slice, three-class CT dataset (non-COVID, COVID, non-informative) along four axes: leakage, shortcuts, external validity and calibration. Replacing a random slice split with a group split on recovered pseudo-patients lowers accuracy from 99.42% to 97.18%, and to 95.39% when groups follow file order. The error rate rises 4.9 to 8.0 times, and recall of COVID slices falls from 99.6% to 96.0% and 88.8%. Scalar acquisition features alone reach 0.996 balanced accuracy under a slice split and 0.630 under a group split (chance 0.333), and models trained without the lungs, or with only the lungs, both reach about 93%. On two external sites, discrimination drops (AUROC 0.83 on Sao Paulo; 0.86 for COVID lesion slices against normal patients in Tehran), and every model scores community-acquired pneumonia as more COVID-like than COVID (AUROC 0.43 to 0.49). Calibration does not transfer: binary ECE rises from 0.02 in-domain to 0.19 to 0.53 externally, and temperature scaling recovers at most 0.034. Because the main dataset has no patient IDs, we tested our grouping against true IDs on the Tehran cohort. It recovers patients poorly (adjusted Rand index at most 0.29). A nearest-neighbor probe scores 0.998 under a random slice split, 0.551 under a true patient split and 0.717 under our recovered groups, so the slice-versus-group gaps we report are lower bounds on true patient-level leakage.

title: Adult Cervical Deformity: Contemporary Evaluation, Classification, and Surgical Decision-Making.
abstract: ➢ Standing full-spine radiographs are mandatory for cervical deformity evaluation; key alignment targets include cervical sagittal vertical axis (cSVA) of ≤40 mm, T1 slope minus cervical lordosis (T1S - CL) of <15°, and a chin-brow vertical angle (CBVA) between -10° and +10° relative to the true vertical. The achievement of these thresholds is independently associated with better patient-reported outcomes, whereas values outside these ranges are associated with worse disability and quality-of-life scores.➢ The Kim-International Spine Study Group (ISSG) morphology-based classification, which identifies 4 patterns (flat neck, focal, cervicothoracic, and coronal or complex) from standing and dynamic extension radiographs, provides a reproducible morphology and flexibility-based framework that informs operative planning and has demonstrated superior interrater and intrarater reliability over prior descriptive systems; final surgical decisions integrate flexibility, neurological status, global alignment, bone quality, and patient-specific factors, and the direct impact of this classification on surgical outcomes requires further prospective validation.➢ Surgical planning is stratified by the intended lower instrumented vertebra (LIV) (Type 1: LIV T2-T4; Type 2: within the cervical spine or cervicothoracic junction; Type 3: extending past the thoracolumbar junction) and by whether the deformity is ankylosed, which determines the need for osteotomy.➢ Overall complication rates exceed 50% in prospective multicenter data; systematic risk mitigation, including neuromonitoring, tranexamic acid, staged approaches, and frailty-based patient selection, is essential for safe outcomes.➢ Despite high complication rates, the surgical correction of cervical deformity yields clinically meaningful improvements in pain and health-related quality of life at 1 year in appropriately selected patients; realistic goal-setting and individualized alignment targets are the keys to durable success.

title: Temporal Macrophage Activation Is Reduced by CCR2 Knockout in a Murine Subacromial Impingement Model.
abstract: Background Rotator cuff (RC) tendinopathy is a prevalent cause of shoulder pain and disability, yet its underlying molecular drivers remain poorly defined. Increasing evidence highlights the role of early inflammation and macrophage activation in symptom development and disease progression. C-C chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) regulates monocyte recruitment and pro-inflammatory macrophage signaling in tendinopathy. This study characterizes the temporal inflammatory profile of RC tendinopathy and evaluates the impact of CCR2 knockout in a murine subacromial impingement (SAI) model. Methods Sixty mice (40 C57BL/6J wild type [WT SAI] and 20 CCR2 knockout [CCR2KO]) underwent bilateral placement of a subacromial surgical clip to induce RC impingement. Four additional C57BL/6J mice underwent sham surgery (WT sham controls). Animals were assessed through 42 days. Macrophage activation was quantified using microPET/CT (micro-positron emission tomography/computed tomography) and gallium-68-labeled folate receptor ligand. Selected WT SAI mice were killed at early and intermediate time points for temporal gene expression profiling. The remaining mice were killed on day 42 for histological, biomechanical, or gene expression analyses. Results WT SAI mice demonstrated a reproducible pattern of early macrophage activation, peaking on postoperative days 3 and 7. CCR2KO mice exhibited significantly reduced macrophage activation at these time points. Gene expression analysis of WT SAI supraspinatus tendons revealed early upregulation of inflammatory and M1 macrophage-related genes, followed by later increases in anti-inflammatory mediators and M2 macrophage-related markers. CCR2KO tendons demonstrated fewer tendinopathic changes on histology but did not exhibit superior biomechanical properties compared with WT SAI tendons. Conclusions RC tendinopathy exhibits a distinct early inflammatory phase characterized by macrophage activation and M1 macrophage-dominant signaling. CCR2KO reduces early inflammatory activity and may attenuate tendon degeneration. Clinical relevance Defining the inflammatory progression of RC disease may help to refine treatment strategies-particularly the use and timing of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroid injections, and emerging biologic therapies. CCR2 represents a potential therapeutic target for modulating early inflammation and improving tendon healing.

title: Core Muscle Injury: A Combined Orthopaedic and General Surgery Algorithmic Approach for Diagnosis, Imaging, and Treatment.
abstract: » Core muscle injury (CMI) is a common cause of groin pain in athletes and reflects pathology of the inguinal canal, rectus abdominis-adductor longus (RA-AL) aponeurosis, and pubic symphysis. » There is a substantial lack of consensus on terminology and diagnostic criteria for CMI, hindering standardized evaluation, management, and research initiatives. » Diagnosis relies on structured history, physical examinations, and provocative maneuvers to identify CMI and concurrent pathology, and fluid-sensitive pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterize RA-AL injury. » Treatment strategies differ across sports medicine physicians, general surgeons, and orthopaedic surgeons, underscoring the need for early cross-departmental referrals to ensure all contributing pathologies are comprehensively identified and addressed. » When both adductor/RA-AL aponeurosis and inguinal canal/abdominal wall pathologies are present, prioritizing collaborative cases between orthopaedic and general surgeons is essential for decreasing operating room time, streamlining rehabilitation, and optimizing return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Proximal Scaphoid Pole Reconstruction Utilizing Ipsilateral Proximal Hamate Autograft.
abstract: Background Proximal pole scaphoid fractures complicated by nonunion and osteonecrosis present a challenging scenario with few good reconstructive options, especially when the proximal fragment is small or fragmented 1-4 . The use of an ipsilateral proximal hamate osteochondral autograft has emerged as a promising technique for reconstructing the proximal scaphoid pole, with the potential to restore carpal mechanics while avoiding the morbidity associated with free vascularized bone grafts or distant autograft sites. Description The procedure involves replacing the diseased proximal scaphoid with a structurally matched osteochondral graft from the ipsilateral proximal hamate. After excising the necrotic or fragmented scaphoid pole, a size-matched graft-harvested with its attached volar capitohamate ligament-is rotated 180° on its longitudinal axis to replicate normal scaphoid anatomy. The defect is measured in 3 planes using the scapholunate joint (proximal) and viable distal scaphoid surface as boundaries. On the hamate, an osteotomy is marked 8 to 10 mm distal to its proximal tip, parallel to the articular surface. The volar capitohamate ligament is preserved to guide graft orientation and maintain stability. These measurements align with recent anatomic and biomechanical studies that have confirmed 6 to 10-mm grafts accurately reproduce scaphoid morphology without compromising carpal kinematics. The graft is then inserted into the defect and secured with rigid internal fixation (headless compression screws or Kirschner wires). Residual gaps may be filled with cancellous bone graft. Scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) reconstruction is typically performed by suturing the hamate's volar capitohamate ligament to the dorsal SLIL remnant on the lunate with a 2-0 nonabsorbable suture. In patients with a partially intact SLIL, such as after failed fixation, the hamate graft alone may provide adequate stability, making formal reconstruction unnecessary. If intraoperative findings reveal dorsal scapholunate instability or an attenuated SLIL, reconstruction is indicated. Healthy, tensionable ligament remnants are repaired directly or reinforced with suture anchors. When dorsal fibers are deficient but volar remnants remain, the attached volar capitohamate ligament is used for reinforcement. For small defects, a micro-interference screw may be employed for fixation. Postoperatively, the wrist is immobilized in a cast. When radiographic evidence of union is observed, the cast is removed and the patient begins a structured hand therapy program. Alternatives Alternatives include vascularized and nonvascularized bone grafts (e.g., iliac crest), a vascularized medial femoral trochlear osteochondral flap, costochondral rib graft, proximal row carpectomy, and wrist arthrodesis 1,2 . These may be limited by donor-site morbidity, complexity, or suboptimal restoration of wrist biomechanics. The use of an ipsilateral proximal hamate osteochondral autograft has emerged as a promising technique for reconstructing the proximal scaphoid pole, with the potential to restore carpal mechanics while avoiding the morbidity associated with free vascularized bone grafts or distant autograft sites.

Description

The procedure involves replacing the diseased proximal scaphoid with a structurally matched osteochondral graft from the ipsilateral proximal hamate. After excising the necrotic or fragmented scaphoid pole, a size-matched graft-harvested with its attached volar capitohamate ligament-is rotated 180° on its longitudinal axis to replicate normal scaphoid anatomy. The defect is measured in 3 planes using the scapholunate joint (proximal) and viable distal scaphoid surface as boundaries. On the hamate, an osteotomy is marked 8 to 10 mm distal to its proximal tip, parallel to the articular surface. The volar capitohamate ligament is preserved to guide graft orientation and maintain stability. These measurements align with recent anatomic and biomechanical studies that have confirmed 6 to 10-mm grafts accurately reproduce scaphoid morphology without compromising carpal kinematics. The graft is then inserted into the defect and secured with rigid internal fixation (headless compression screws or Kirschner wires). Residual gaps may be filled with cancellous bone graft. Scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) reconstruction is typically performed by suturing the hamate's volar capitohamate ligament to the dorsal SLIL remnant on the lunate with a 2-0 nonabsorbable suture. In patients with a partially intact SLIL, such as after failed fixation, the hamate graft alone may provide adequate stability, making formal reconstruction unnecessary. If intraoperative findings reveal dorsal scapholunate instability or an attenuated SLIL, reconstruction is indicated. Healthy, tensionable ligament remnants are repaired directly or reinforced with suture anchors. When dorsal fibers are deficient but volar remnants remain, the attached volar capitohamate ligament is used for reinforcement. For small defects, a micro-interference screw may be employed for fixation. Postoperatively, the wrist is immobilized in a cast. title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
abstract: Background Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading 1,2 . High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery 3,4 . Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery. Description The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion. Alternatives Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization 5,6 . Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern 2,7,8 . Rationale This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport. Expected outcomes Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport 8 . Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients 6,7 . Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence. Important tips The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics. title: Co-occurrence of spinocerebellar ataxia type 16 and IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma associated with compound heterozygous STUB1 variants: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background : Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia type 16 (SCAR16), caused by biallelic STUB1 variants, is a rare cerebellar degenerative disorder. While STUB1 (encoding CHIP) is increasingly recognized as a tumor suppressor in gliomas, the co-occurrence of SCAR16 and intracranial glioma has not been systematically reported. This study aims to characterize the clinical, radiological, and genetic features of this unique comorbidity and explore the underlying pathogenic mechanisms. Case presentation: We report a 35-year-old woman with a 7-year history of progressive gait ataxia. Initial cranial MRI revealed diffuse cerebellar atrophy. Whole-exome sequencing identified compound heterozygous STUB1 variants: a nonsense mutation (c.352C>T, p.Gln118Ter) and a missense mutation (c.433A>C, p.Lys145Gln), confirmed by familial segregation analysis. At age 33, serial MRI detected a new right temporal lobe lesion. Surgical resection was performed, and histopathology confirmed a WHO grade 2 IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma. Postoperatively, the patient received adjuvant temozolomide chemotherapy. Conclusions: This case provides the first clinical evidence linking biallelic STUB1 loss-of-function to both neurodegeneration and gliomagenesis. We propose a dual-pathway model wherein STUB1 deficiency impairs neuronal protein quality control (leading to cerebellar atrophy) and relieves tumor-suppressor restraint in glial cells (increasing susceptibility to IDH-mutant glioma). These findings expand the phenotypic spectrum of STUB1-related disorders and underscore the necessity of genetic screening in adult-onset ataxia with atypical features.

title: Deep learning integrated clinical-radiomics model for prognostic prediction in locally advanced cervical cancer through 18 F-FDG PET/CT and MRI combination
abstract: Abstract Background Precise pretreatment risk stratification is critical for guiding treatment intensification and personalized follow‑up in patients with locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC) after concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT). This study developed and validated a deep learning integrated clinical-radiomics model for prognosis prediction in patients with LACC treated with CCRT, using dual-modal pretreatment imaging from 18 F-FDG PET/CT and contrast-enhanced MRI. Methods We retrospectively collected 346 patients (276 for training and 70 for testing) with LACC between June 2016 and October 2021. Radiomics and deep learning signatures were extracted from PET/CT and MRI. These signatures were integrated with the clinicopathological factors into a nomogram for clinical applications. Models were constructed using eleven machine learning algorithms, and a clinical-radiomics-deep learning model (CRDLM) was developed. The evaluation of the model’s performance was conducted through the metrics of the area under the curve (AUC). Results The CRDLM demonstrated superior predictive performance (AUCs of 0.998 (95% CI: 1.00–1.00) for training cohort and 0.901 (95% CI: 0.83–0.97) for testing cohort), which is significantly superior to conventional clinical factors (FIGO stage and SCC-Ag, AUC = 0.605–0.658). In addition, the CRDLM which combined radiomics with deep learning significantly outperformed the radiomics‑only model (AUC = 0.793, p = 0.006). Sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of CRDLM reached 0.947, 0.725, and 0.786, respectively. Conclusions The CRDLM provides robust prediction of disease progression in LACC patients who received CCRT, which may facilitate personalized treatment strategies and improve clinical outcomes. Further validation in multicenter prospective studies is warranted.

title: MESO-FAP: Protocol for a Phase 1a/1b Study of [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 Radioligand Therapy Combined with Nivolumab and Ipilimumab in Advanced Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma
abstract: Abstract Background Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) remains an aggressive malignancy associated with poor prognosis despite advances in systemic therapy. Dual immune checkpoint blockade with nivolumab and ipilimumab has improved survival outcomes and is established as a first-line treatment option for unresectable disease; however, durable responses occur in only a subset of patients, and treatment resistance remains common. Increasing evidence implicates the tumour microenvironment, particularly cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and stromal-mediated immune exclusion, as important contributors to therapeutic resistance. Fibroblast activation protein (FAP), highly expressed on activated CAFs within mesothelioma stroma, represents a promising theranostic target. FAP-directed radioligand therapy using [ 177 Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 has demonstrated favourable tumour targeting and encouraging preclinical anti-tumour activity and may enhance anti-tumour immunity through modulation of the tumour microenvironment. Results MESO-FAP is an investigator-initiated multicentre phase 1a/1b study evaluating [ 177 Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 in combination with nivolumab and ipilimumab in patients with unresectable or advanced malignant pleural mesothelioma. The study comprises a dose-escalation phase using a conventional 3 + 3 design followed by a dose-expansion cohort. Eligible participants must demonstrate FAP-positive disease on screening [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAP-2286 PET/CT. Primary endpoints include safety, dose-limiting toxicities, determination of the maximum tolerated dose, and establishment of the recommended phase 2 dose. Secondary and exploratory endpoints include treatment response, survival outcomes, radiation dosimetry, molecular imaging biomarkers, and integrated translational analyses incorporating tissue and blood-based biomarkers. Conclusions MESO-FAP is the first prospective study investigating FAP-targeted radioligand therapy combined with dual immune checkpoint blockade in mesothelioma. The study incorporates a theranostic framework integrating molecular imaging, dosimetry, and translational biomarker analyses to establish the safety profile and recommended Phase 2 dose of stromal-directed radio-immunotherapy in MPM while generating mechanistic insights to guide future biomarker-driven clinical development. Trial registration Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR), ACTRN12626000505303. Registered 23 April 2026, https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?id=391496&isReview=true

title: Towards UASC-Net: A Pilot Study of Uncertainty-Aware 3D Brain Tumor Segmentation on BraTS 2021
abstract: Abstract Brain tumor segmentation from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a central component of treatment planning and disease monitoring, but reliable voxel-wise annotation is costly and difficult to obtain. This work presents a pilot evaluation of UASC-Net Lite v2, an uncertainty-aware extension of a compact 3D U-Net baseline for binary tumor segmentation from multimodal BraTS 2021 MRI patches. The model combines a 3D encoder–decoder segmentation pathway with attention-, prototype-, and uncertainty-related auxiliary outputs, enabling spatial confidence inspection alongside mask prediction. Experiments were conducted on a reproducible 16-case pilot subset (13 training and 3 validation cases), using 64×64×64 patches and eight training epochs. After validation-set threshold calibration, the proposed model achieved a pooled Dice score of 0.7381 and IoU of 0.5849, compared with 0.7297 and 0.5744 for the TinyUNet3D baseline. UASC-Net Lite v2 improved sensitivity from 0.7681 to 0.8609, while specificity and precision changed from 0.9685 and 0.6949 to 0.9532 and 0.6460, respectively. Qualitative visualizations show the segmentation outputs together with uncertainty and attention maps. These results should be interpreted as a pilot study rather than a full benchmark: threshold calibration was performed on the validation patches and the cohort is small. Nevertheless, the experiment provides reproducible evidence that uncertainty-aware modeling can improve lesion recall and overlap under limited-data conditions.

title: Poorly Differentiated Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Regaud–Schmincke Type of the Posterior Pharyngeal Wall: Diagnostic Challenges and Pitfalls
abstract: Abstract Background: Oropharyngeal tumors may initially present with nonspecific inflammatory symptoms, leading to diagnostic delay. Large exophytic lesions of the posterior pharyngeal wall are uncommon and may clinically and radiologically mimic infectious or inflammatory conditions. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 67-year-old male presenting with progressive dysphagia, intermittent dysphonia, and foreign body sensation in the throat. Initial clinical evaluation and histopathological examination suggested an inflammatory process. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a large polypoid mass arising from the posterior pharyngeal wall, extending to the left salpingopharyngeal fold and the hypopharynx, with craniocaudal extension of approximately 64 mm and significant airway narrowing. Repeat biopsy followed by surgical excision confirmed poorly differentiated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the Regaud–Schmincke type with deep soft-tissue infiltration, including invasion of striated muscle and salivary gland parenchyma. Due to impending airway obstruction, protective tracheostomy was performed prior to surgery. The postoperative course was complicated by transient acute kidney injury, which resolved with conservative management. The patient subsequently completed adjuvant external beam radiotherapy and was successfully decannulated four months postoperatively. Follow-up imaging demonstrated no evidence of local recurrence or distant metastasis. Conclusion: This case highlights the diagnostic challenges posed by exophytic oropharyngeal carcinomas presenting with inflammatory features and underscores the importance of cross-sectional imaging and repeat histopathological evaluation in patients with persistent or progressive pharyngeal symptoms.
